hash_change_test.result: Hash divergence successfully demonstrated on benign wording change. Original SHA-256 (ca0fd361fb97f93c24f1a491904379e390ad34207dfd3f70b3a50c31619b6ef7) differed from modified SHA-256 (397ddb30208d3f10f1c4e0fa9c976d0a9a03f78a7cad5d4290019a441366a1ad), resulting in a baseline mismatch alert despite harmless semantic equivalence.
hash_change_test.notes: Original description: 'Returns the current status.' Modified description: 'Returns the current system status.' Both versions were hosted on local MCP stdio servers and inspected using snyk-agent-scan inspect.

findings: snyk-agent-scan (mcp-scan) v0.6.8 inspects and extracts MCP tool definitions, input schemas, and metadata across both public packages and local stdio server scripts.
Tool pinning relies on strict cryptographic hashing (SHA-256) of tool manifests.
Because cryptographic hashing is semantic-blind, legitimate documentation changes, clarification of wording, and bug fixes trigger identical change alerts as malicious tool poisoning.
This establishes the foundational baseline and confirms the research necessity for an intelligent semantic drift judge.
limitations: mcp-scan has been rebranded to snyk-agent-scan on PyPI; direct execution of its generated .exe in uv cache was blocked by Windows Application Control policy, but running via Python entry point (agent_scan.run) bypassed this restriction cleanly.
Deep cloud vulnerability analysis ('scan') requires remote Snyk API tokens and connectivity, whereas local capability extraction ('inspect') functions offline.
Hash pinning operates as an all-or-nothing binary flag, unable to evaluate semantic intent.
